the nuclear calcium response of a CA1 neuron to synaptic stimulation is enhanced by repeated stimulation and that this enhancement is required for the induction of late long-term potentiation.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular and cellular mechanisms that control synaptic plasticity and the dialogue between synapses and nuclei in the hippocampus.
the molecular and cellular mechanisms of synaptic plasticity and memory.
the mechanisms by which synaptic activity regulates gene expression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

nuclear calcium transients are not a reliable readout of the number of action potential spikes generated by synaptic activity, but that they are a reliable readout for the number of action spikes generated by the same activity when it is repeated.

the amplitude and duration of activity-dependent nuclear calcium signals in CA1 pyralmal neurons are regulated by the number of action potential spikes evoked by synaptic stimulation, and by repetition-induced amplification of action potential firing and nuclear calcium signaling.
nuclear calcium signaling is a key signal that regulates transcription-dependent LTP.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the nuclear calcium signals induced by a single train of high-frequency stimulation (1 Hz) are not sufficient to induce transcription-dependent late-LTP.

the magnitude of activity-induced nuclear calcium signals is greatly amplified by the repetition of stimulation trains, and this may be an important mechanism for triggering the transcription-dependent phase of late LTP.
nuclear calcium signaling can be used to identify and characterize the synaptic inputs that trigger L-LTP.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a repetition-induced switch in synaptic input and nuclear output is a key component in the dialogue between the synapse and nucleus, which controls the genomic responses underlying memory and neuroprotection.
the magnitude of activity-induced nuclear calcium signals depends on the number of action potential spikes generated during synaptic stimulation trains.
the magnitude and duration of nuclear Ca2+ signaling is greatly amplified when the synaptic activity is repeated.
